tool.name: grep, sed & awk
tool.tagline: The classic Unix trio for searching, editing and summarising text
tool.description: grep finds lines, sed edits them as they stream past and awk splits them into fields and computes with them. Together with sort, uniq, cut and xargs they turn logs, CSVs and config files into answers in one pipeline, on any Unix machine, without writing a program.

glossary.def: A program that reads text from standard input or files, changes it, and writes the result to standard output, so it can sit in the middle of a pipeline.
The project that makes the standard versions of grep, sed, awk (gawk) and many other command-line tools found on Linux.
A family of Unix-like systems whose command-line tools macOS also uses; they differ from the GNU versions on Linux in some options.
GNU awk: the most feature-rich version of awk, standard on many Linux systems, with extras other awks lack.
A small, fast version of awk, used as the default awk on Debian and Ubuntu; it lacks most gawk extras.
One small program that provides simplified versions of many standard commands (grep, sed, awk...), used in tiny Linux systems such as Alpine.
A set of characters in square brackets in a pattern, like [0-9] or [[:space:]], that matches any one character from the set.
The default pattern style of grep and sed, in which + ? | ( ) { } are plain characters unless you put a backslash before them.
The pattern style of grep -E and sed -E, in which + ? | ( ) { } have their special meaning without backslashes.
sed's work area: the current line (or lines) that sed's commands act on before printing it and moving on.
A second storage area in sed that keeps text from one line to the next, used for edits that span several lines.
The part before a sed command saying which lines it applies to: a line number, $ for the last line, a /pattern/ or a range of them.
In awk, one unit of input, normally one line, which awk splits into fields.
A part of a pattern in parentheses whose matched text is remembered, so the replacement can reuse it.
A code like \1 that stands for the text a capture group matched, used in a replacement or later in the same pattern.
The character with code 0. It can never appear in a file name, so tools use it to separate names safely.
Perl-compatible regular expressions: the richer pattern style of the Perl language, with \d, lookarounds and more; grep -P uses it.
A part of a pattern that checks what comes just before or after the match without including it in the match.
A fast modern search tool like grep -r that skips ignored, hidden and non-text files by default and uses all processor cores.
In awk, input text that looks like a number (a field, for example), so it compares as a number with other numbers.
awk with RS set to an empty string: records are separated by blank lines instead of line breaks.
Deterministic finite automaton: a lookup table built from a pattern that checks text one byte at a time without ever going back.
A matching method that tries one way to match and, if it fails, goes back to try another; it can become extremely slow on some patterns.

concepts.name: Text streams and the filter model
concepts.summary: Treat text as a stream of lines flowing through small filters: grep picks lines, sed edits them, awk splits them into fields and calculates.
concepts.why: Knowing which tool does which job is what lets you answer questions about log files and data files in one line.
concepts.body:
Programs you run in the terminal on Linux and macOS, which grew out of an older system called Unix, agree on one simple data format: **text as a stream of lines**. A **filter** is a program that reads lines from standard input (or from files named as arguments), changes them and writes lines to standard output. Because every filter speaks the same format, you can chain them with pipes, and each one stays small.

The three classics each have a job:

- `grep` **selects** lines that match a pattern and drops the rest.
- `sed` **edits** lines as they stream past: replace text, delete lines, insert lines.
- `awk` splits each line into **fields**, the separate words or columns on the line, and runs a small program on them: keep rows by the value in a column, add numbers up, count, reformat.

Around them sit helpers you'll use constantly: `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `head`, `tail`, `wc` and `xargs`.

On Linux these tools come from the **GNU** project. macOS ships slightly different versions, so a few options marked "GNU" in these lessons won't work there.

A lot of the text you'll process is **logging** output: the text files where programs write down what they did, one event per line. A good habit is to build a pipeline one stage at a time. Run the first command, look at the output (pipe into `head` while exploring), then add the next stage. Each stage is easy to test on its own, and when something goes wrong you can remove stages from the end until the output looks right again.

None of these tools change their input file unless you explicitly ask (for example `sed -i`). They read, transform and print, so experimenting is safe.
concepts.code:
printf 'GET /home 200\nPOST /login 401\nGET /home 200\nGET /api 500\n' > access.log

grep 'GET' access.log                 # select: the three GET lines
sed 's/GET/get/' access.log           # edit: lower-case the first word on every line
awk '{ print $3 }' access.log         # fields: 200 401 200 500

# combined: which paths returned 200, and how often?
grep ' 200$' access.log | awk '{ print $2 }' | sort | uniq -c
#       2 /home
takeaways: grep selects lines, sed edits lines, awk works with fields
Filters read standard input or files and write standard output, so they chain with pipes
Build pipelines stage by stage, checking the output each time
pitfalls: Reaching for awk or a script when a single grep would do, or chaining five greps when one awk would be clearer.

quiz.q: You need the total of the third column of a file whose columns are separated by spaces. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explain: awk splits lines into fields and can keep a running sum, which grep and sed cannot do naturally.

concepts.name: grep: finding lines
concepts.summary: Search files or input for lines matching a pattern, with the everyday flags -i, -v, -n, -c, -w, -l and -r.
concepts.why: grep is the fastest way to find where something is mentioned, in one file or across a whole project.
concepts.body:
`grep PATTERN [FILE...]` prints every line containing a match for `PATTERN`. With no file it reads standard input, so it works at the end of any pipeline. Quote the pattern in single quotes so the shell leaves it alone.

The options you'll use daily:

- `-i` ignore upper/lower case; `-v` invert: print lines that do **not** match.
- `-n` put line numbers in front; `-c` print only the count of matching lines.
- `-w` match whole words only, so `-w cat` skips `concatenate`.
- `-l` list only the names of files that contain a match.
- `-e PAT` adds a pattern (you can repeat it; also needed for patterns starting with `-`).

`-r` searches a whole **directory** (another word for folder), including every folder inside it. `-R` does the same but also follows **symbolic links**: shortcut-like files that point to another file or folder.

When several files are searched, grep puts the file name in front of each line; `-h` hides it and `-H` forces it. With `-r`, narrow the search with `--include='*.py'`, `--exclude='*.min.js'` and `--exclude-dir=node_modules`.

By default the pattern is a regular expression, so characters such as `.` and `*` are special. If you're searching for exact text, use `-F` (fixed strings): it's faster, and you can't be surprised by a stray dot.

Options combine freely: `grep -rniw todo src/` finds TODOs in the `src` folder, in any case, as whole words, with file names and line numbers.
concepts.code:
printf 'apple pie\nbanana split\nApple tart\ncherry pie\n' > menu.txt

grep apple menu.txt          # apple pie
grep -i apple menu.txt       # apple pie / Apple tart
grep -v pie menu.txt         # banana split / Apple tart
grep -c pie menu.txt         # 2
grep -n cherry menu.txt      # 4:cherry pie
grep -F 'pie' menu.txt       # exact text, no special characters

# search a project folder: only Python files, skipping the .venv folder
grep -rn --include='*.py' --exclude-dir=.venv 'import requests' .
grep -rl 'TODO' src/         # just the file names
takeaways: -i ignore case, -v invert, -n line numbers, -c count, -w whole word
-r searches folders; narrow it with --include and --exclude-dir
-F treats the pattern as exact text: faster and no surprises
pitfalls: Forgetting to quote the pattern, so the shell expands * or splits words before grep sees them.

quiz.q: What does grep -vc error app.log print?
options: The number of times error appears
Only the word error from each line
The lines that don't contain error
The number of lines that don't contain error
quiz.explain: -v inverts the selection and -c replaces the output with a count of the selected lines.

quiz.q: Why use grep -F '1.5.0' instead of grep '1.5.0'?
options: Without -F grep only matches whole lines
Without -F the dots match any character, so 105a0 would match too
quiz.explain: In a regular expression . matches any character; -F turns that off.

concepts.name: Patterns in grep: BRE and ERE
concepts.summary: Use anchors, character classes and repetition in grep patterns, and know when -E changes which characters are special.
concepts.why: Real searches are rarely for exact text; a few regular expression pieces turn grep into a precise tool.
concepts.body:
grep patterns are regular expressions. The pieces you need first:

- `.` matches any one character.
- A **character class** in square brackets matches one character from a set: `[abc]` one of a, b or c; `[^abc]` anything but those; `[0-9]` any digit. Named sets work everywhere: `[[:digit:]]`, `[[:space:]]`, `[[:alpha:]]`.
- `^` is the start of the line and `$` the end: `^#` finds comment lines, `^$` empty ones.
- `*` repeats the previous item zero or more times.

grep understands two flavours of regular expression. **Basic regular expressions** (BRE, the default) treat `+ ? | ( ) { }` as ordinary characters. To make them special you put a backslash in front: `\+`, `\|`, `\(...\)` (for `\+ \? \|` only GNU grep allows this).

**Extended regular expressions** (ERE, `grep -E`, once called `egrep`) make those characters special without backslashes:

- `+` one or more, `?` optional, `{2,4}` between two and four.
- `a|b` either a or b; `( )` groups pieces together.

Use `-E` whenever your pattern has `|` or repetition; it's far easier to read. `-o` prints only the matched part instead of the whole line, which is handy for pulling out values.

Don't use `\d` for a digit in BRE or ERE: it isn't supported reliably. Write `[0-9]` or `[[:digit:]]`. For the Perl language's style of patterns, with `\d` and more, GNU grep has `-P`, covered later.
concepts.code:
printf 'id=42 ok\nid=7 FAIL\n# comment\n\nid=1234 ok\n' > data.txt

grep '^#' data.txt                         # # comment
grep -c '^$' data.txt                      # 1  (empty lines)
grep 'id=[0-9][0-9]* ok$' data.txt         # id=42 ok / id=1234 ok   (BRE)
grep -E 'id=[0-9]+ (ok|FAIL)' data.txt     # every id line            (ERE)
grep -E 'id=[0-9]{3,}' data.txt            # id=1234 ok
grep -oE '[0-9]+' data.txt                 # 42 / 7 / 1234, one per line

grep 'ok|FAIL' data.txt                    # nothing: | is literal in BRE
grep 'ok\|FAIL' data.txt                   # works in GNU BRE, but prefer -E
takeaways: ^ and $ match the start and end of the line
Use grep -E for + ? | ( ) { } without backslashes
-o prints just the matched text; use [0-9] instead of \d
pitfalls: Writing grep 'a|b' and getting no matches: alternation needs -E (or \| in GNU BRE).

quiz.q: Which command prints lines that consist only of digits?
quiz.explain: Both anchors are needed so the whole line is digits, and + needs -E to mean one or more.

concepts.name: sed: substitution with s///
concepts.summary: Rewrite text on the fly with s/pattern/replacement/flags, using g for every match, & for the matched text, and other separator characters.
concepts.why: Search-and-replace across a stream or a file is the most common text edit in scripts and one-liners.
concepts.body:
`sed` (stream editor) reads its input one line at a time into a work area called the **pattern space**, runs your commands on it, prints the result and moves on to the next line. The command you'll use 90% of the time is substitution:

```bash
sed 's/old/new/' file
```

- Without flags only the **first** match on each line is replaced. Add `g` for all matches, or a number (`2`) for the second only.
- `I` (GNU) makes the match ignore upper and lower case.
- In the replacement, `&` stands for the whole matched text: `s/[0-9]*/<&>/` wraps the number in angle brackets.
- Several commands go in separate `-e` options, or are separated by `;`.

The `/` characters are the **delimiter**: the separator between the parts of the command. It can be any character, so `s|/usr/local|/opt|` saves you from putting a backslash before every slash in a path.

The pattern is a BRE by default, just like grep. Use `sed -E` for ERE, so `+`, `?`, `|` and parentheses work without backslashes.

sed writes to standard output and leaves the input file untouched: send the output to a new file with `>`, or use `-i` (covered later) once you're sure. To put an actual `&` or the delimiter in the replacement, put a backslash before it: `\&`, `\/`.

Remember that `.` in the pattern matches any character, so `s/1.0/2.0/` also changes `100`. Write `1\.0` when you mean a real dot.
concepts.code:
echo 'one cat, two cats, red cat' | sed 's/cat/dog/'
# one dog, two cats, red cat
echo 'one cat, two cats, red cat' | sed 's/cat/dog/g'
# one dog, two dogs, red dog
echo 'one cat, two cats, red cat' | sed 's/cat/dog/2'
# one cat, two dogs, red cat

echo 'price 42' | sed 's/[0-9][0-9]*/[&]/'          # price [42]
echo 'path=/usr/local/bin' | sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|'  # path=/opt/bin
echo 'v1.0 and 100' | sed 's/1\.0/2.0/g'            # v2.0 and 100
echo 'Hello World' | sed -e 's/Hello/Bye/' -e 's/World/all/'   # Bye all
takeaways: s/pattern/replacement/ changes the first match; add g for all
& in the replacement is the whole match
Pick another delimiter (s|a|b|) when the text contains slashes
pitfalls: Expecting s/x/y/ to replace every occurrence on a line; without g only the first changes.

quiz.q: What does echo 'aaa' | sed 's/a/b/2' print?
quiz.explain: The numeric flag 2 replaces only the second match on the line.

concepts.name: awk: fields and printing
concepts.summary: awk splits each line into fields $1 to $NF; print the columns you want, change the separator with -F, and use NR and NF.
concepts.why: Pulling columns out of log files, command output or comma-separated files is awk's bread and butter.
concepts.body:
An awk program is a list of `pattern { action }` rules, run on every input line. awk calls each line a **record**. Each record is split into fields: `$1`, `$2` and so on, while `$0` is the whole line. By default fields are separated by runs of spaces and tabs, and blanks at the start of the line are ignored, which suits command output like `ps` or `ls -l`.

Built-in variables you'll use straight away:

- `NF`: the number of fields on this line, so `$NF` is the last field and `$(NF-1)` the one before it.
- `NR`: the current record number (the line number, counted across all input).
- `-F ','` (or `-F':'`) sets the field separator, `FS`. It can be a single character or a regular expression such as `-F '[,;]'`.

`print a, b` prints its arguments with the output field separator `OFS` between them (a space by default), then a line break. `print a b` (no comma) joins them with nothing in between. To change `OFS`, use `-v OFS='\t'`.

Always put the program in single quotes, so the shell doesn't replace `$1` with its own value first.

Note that `-F ','` doesn't fully understand **CSV** (comma-separated values, the plain-text table format spreadsheets export): a quoted field containing a comma, like `"Smith, Ann"`, gets split in two. For real CSV use gawk's `--csv` option (gawk is GNU awk, version 5.3 or later) or a tool built for CSV.
concepts.code:
printf 'alice 31 london\nbob 25 paris\ncarol 40 rome\n' > people.txt

awk '{ print $1 }' people.txt             # alice / bob / carol
awk '{ print $3, $1 }' people.txt         # london alice ...
awk '{ print NR ": " $1 " is " $2 }' people.txt
# 1: alice is 31 ...
awk '{ print $NF }' people.txt            # last field: london / paris / rome

# fields separated by colons, like the system's user list /etc/passwd
printf 'root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n' | awk -F: '{ print $1, $NF }'
# root /bin/bash

awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, $2 }' people.txt    # tab-separated output
takeaways: $1 to $NF are fields, $0 the whole line, NR the line number
-F sets the input separator; OFS controls what print puts between values
Single-quote the program so the shell leaves $1 alone
pitfalls: Using double quotes around the program: the shell replaces $1 with its own (usually empty) argument.

quiz.q: For the line 'a b c d', what does awk '{ print $(NF-1) }' print?
quiz.explain: NF is 4, so $(NF-1) is $3, the second-to-last field.

quiz.q: What does awk '{ print $1 $2 }' print for the line 'x y'?
quiz.explain: Without a comma, print joins its arguments with nothing in between.

concepts.name: grep output control and scripting
concepts.summary: Show context with -A/-B/-C, stop early with -m, extract matches with -o and use -q with grep's exit status in scripts.
concepts.why: Context lines make log files readable, and grep's exit status is the standard 'does this file contain X?' test in shell scripts.
concepts.body:
When reading logs you usually want the lines around a match. `-A 3` prints three lines **after** each match, `-B 3` three **before**, `-C 3` both. Groups of context are separated by `--` lines.

Other output controls:

- `-m N` stops after N matching lines (per file), which is fast on huge files.
- `-o` prints only the matched parts, one per line; combine it with `-E` to pull out IDs, numbers or web addresses.
- `--color=auto` highlights matches in a terminal.
- `-Z` / `--null` ends each file name with a **NUL** character (character code 0, which can never appear in a file name), for safe use with `xargs -0` (covered later).

grep's **exit status** is designed for scripts: `0` if any line matched, `1` if none matched, `2` on an error such as a missing file. With `-q` (quiet) grep prints nothing and exits at the first match, so it's the standard way to test whether something is there:

```bash
if grep -q '^backup:' /etc/passwd; then echo "user exists"; fi
```

Be careful in scripts that use `set -e` (stop at the first failing command) or `pipefail`: a grep that finds nothing returns 1, which counts as a failure. If "no matches" is fine, write `grep ... || true`.

`-s` hides messages about files that can't be read, useful with broad `-r` searches.
concepts.code:
printf 'start\nload config\nERROR disk full\nretry\nok\nERROR timeout\n' > app.log

grep -B1 -A1 ERROR app.log
# load config
# ERROR disk full
# retry
# --
# ok
# ERROR timeout

grep -m1 ERROR app.log                  # ERROR disk full
grep -oE 'ERROR [a-z]+' app.log         # ERROR disk / ERROR timeout

if grep -q 'timeout' app.log; then
  echo "saw a timeout"                  # saw a timeout
fi
grep -q 'panic' app.log; echo "status $?"   # status 1
takeaways: -A/-B/-C add context lines after, before or around matches
Exit status: 0 = matched, 1 = no match, 2 = error
grep -q inside an if is the standard presence test
pitfalls: A grep with no matches stopping a set -e script; add || true when an empty result is acceptable.

quiz.q: A script runs grep -q pattern file. Which exit status means the file exists but contains no match?
quiz.explain: grep returns 1 for no match and reserves 2 for errors such as a missing file.

concepts.name: sed addresses, ranges and commands
concepts.summary: Choose which lines a sed command applies to with line numbers, patterns and ranges, and use d, p, -n, i, a and c.
concepts.why: Addresses turn sed from a global search-and-replace into a precise editor for settings files and generated text.
concepts.body:
Every sed command can be prefixed by an **address** that selects the lines it applies to:

- a line number `3`, the last line `$`, or a pattern `/^#/`;
- a range `5,10`, `/BEGIN/,/END/` (from a line matching BEGIN to the next line matching END), or `/start/,+2`;
- `!` after the address reverses it: `/^#/!` means lines that are not comments.

Useful commands besides `s`:

- `d` deletes the line (it isn't printed).
- `p` prints the pattern space. sed prints every line automatically, so `p` is normally used with `-n`, which turns automatic printing off: `sed -n '10,20p'` prints only lines 10 to 20.
- `q` quits: `sed 5q` is a fast `head -n 5`.
- `i\ text`, `a\ text` and `c\ text` insert a line before, append one after, or replace the line. GNU sed also accepts the one-line form `a text`.
- `=` prints the line number.

Commands can be grouped with braces. In an INI-style settings file (sections headed `[name]`, then `key=value` lines), `/^\[db\]/,/^\[/{ s/^port=.*/port=5433/ }` changes `port` only inside the `[db]` section.

A pattern range starts on the first matching line and ends on the next line matching the end pattern; if the end pattern never matches, the range runs to the end of the input.
concepts.code:
printf '# settings\nname=demo\n[db]\nport=5432\n[web]\nport=8080\n' > app.ini

sed -n '2,3p' app.ini            # name=demo / [db]
sed '/^#/d' app.ini              # everything except the comment
sed -n '/^\[db\]/,/^\[/p' app.ini
# [db]
# port=5432
# [web]

# change port only inside the [db] section
sed '/^\[db\]/,/^\[/ s/^port=.*/port=5433/' app.ini | grep port
# port=5433
# port=8080

sed '1a\
# generated, do not edit' app.ini | head -2     # adds a line after line 1
sed -n '$=' app.ini              # 6  (number of the last line)
takeaways: Addresses: line numbers, $, /pattern/, ranges a,b and reversal with !
sed -n plus p prints only the lines you select
d deletes, q quits, i/a/c insert, append and change lines
pitfalls: Using p without -n and seeing every selected line printed twice.

quiz.q: What does sed -n '/start/,/end/p' print?
options: Each block from a start line through the next end line
Only lines containing start or end
quiz.explain: A pattern range selects from a matching start line to the next end line, and p prints the selection.

concepts.name: Capture groups and in-place editing
concepts.summary: Reorder text with sed -E capture groups and \1 backreferences, and edit files safely with -i and a backup suffix.
concepts.why: Most real sed jobs rearrange parts of a line and then save the result back into the file.
concepts.body:
Parentheses in the pattern make a **capture group**: they remember what they matched. In the replacement, a **backreference** `\1` to `\9` inserts what the first to ninth group captured. In BRE the parentheses need backslashes, so use `sed -E` (ERE) and write plain `( )`:

```bash
sed -E 's/([a-z]+)@([a-z.]+)/\2: \1/'
```

GNU sed can also change case in the replacement: `\U` upper-cases what follows, `\L` lower-cases, `\E` stops; `\u` and `\l` affect only the next character.

To change a file in place use `-i`. GNU sed writes a temporary file and renames it over the original. Give a suffix to keep a copy of the original: `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file` leaves `file.bak` behind.

This is where versions differ. macOS uses **BSD** sed, from another family of Unix-like systems, and there `-i` **requires** a suffix, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` fails; the empty suffix is written `sed -i '' ...`. The form `-i.bak` (no space) works on both GNU and BSD sed, so prefer it in shared scripts, then delete the copy if you don't need it.

Before running `-i` on many files, preview the change without `-i`, or compare old and new with `diff`. And because `-i` replaces the file with a new one, it can change who owns the file in some cases, which matters for files edited as root (the administrator account).
concepts.code:
echo 'alice@example.com' | sed -E 's/([a-z]+)@([a-z.]+)/\2: \1/'
# example.com: alice

echo '2026-10-17' | sed -E 's/([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})/\3.\2.\1/'
# 17.10.2026

echo 'hello world' | sed -E 's/(\w+)/\u\1/g'     # Hello World (GNU)

printf 'debug=true\nlevel=3\n' > app.conf
sed -i.bak 's/^debug=true/debug=false/' app.conf   # works with GNU and BSD sed
cat app.conf          # debug=false / level=3
cat app.conf.bak      # debug=true  / level=3
diff app.conf.bak app.conf    # shows the one changed line
takeaways: sed -E lets you write ( ) for groups; \1 to \9 reuse them in the replacement
-i edits in place; -i.bak keeps a copy and works on BSD/macOS too
Preview without -i before rewriting many files
pitfalls: Running sed -i 's/x/y/' file on macOS, where the s/// command is taken as the backup suffix and the command fails.

quiz.q: What does echo 'b a' | sed -E 's/(.) (.)/\2 \1/' print?
quiz.explain: The two captured characters are written back in swapped order.

concepts.name: awk patterns, BEGIN and END
concepts.summary: Pick records with comparisons and regular expressions, and use BEGIN and END blocks to set up and report.
concepts.why: Patterns let one awk command replace a grep plus a cut, and END blocks turn a filter into a report.
concepts.code:
printf 'name dept salary\nana eng 120\nbo ops 80\ncy eng 95\n' > staff.txt

awk 'NR > 1 && $3 > 90' staff.txt            # ana eng 120 / cy eng 95
awk '$2 ~ /^e/ { print $1 }' staff.txt       # ana / cy

awk 'BEGIN { print "Report" }
     NR > 1 { total += $3; n++ }
     END    { printf "%d people, avg %.1f\n", n, total / n }' staff.txt
# Report
# 3 people, avg 98.3

awk 'END { print NR " lines" }' staff.txt    # 4 lines
takeaways: pattern { action }: no action prints the line, no pattern matches every line
~ and !~ match a field against a regular expression
BEGIN runs before input, END after it; new variables start as 0 or empty
pitfalls: Forgetting to skip the header line (NR > 1) and having it counted or summed.

quiz.q: What does awk '$2 > 10' file do?
options: Prints field 2 if it is over 10
Prints whole lines whose second field is over 10
quiz.explain: A pattern with no action uses the default action, which prints the whole record.

concepts.name: Counting and grouping with awk arrays
concepts.summary: Use awk's associative arrays to count, sum and group by a key, and loop over the results in END.
concepts.why: Group-by summaries of log files and CSV exports are among the most useful one-liners you can write.
concepts.body:
An **array** holds many values, each stored under its own **index** (or key). awk arrays are **associative arrays**: the index can be any text, not just a position number, like words in a dictionary. That makes grouping easy. `count[$1]++` adds one to a counter for the value in column 1, creating it on first use. `sum[$2] += $3` keeps a running total per key.

To report, loop over the keys in `END`:

```awk
END { for (k in sum) print k, sum[k] }
```

The order of `for (k in arr)` is **not defined**. Pipe the output into `sort` (for example `sort -k2,2nr` sorts by the second column, as numbers, largest first), or in gawk set `PROCINFO["sorted_in"] = "@ind_str_asc"` before the loop.

Other array tools:

- `(key in arr)` tests whether a key exists without creating it; `arr[key] == ""` would create it.
- `delete arr[key]` removes one element; `delete arr` empties the array. That's part of **POSIX**, the official common rules for Unix-like tools, since 2024, and has worked everywhere for years.
- Keys made of several parts: `arr[$1, $2]` joins the parts with the special character in `SUBSEP`.

A classic trick is `!seen[$0]++`, a pattern that is true the first time a line is seen: `awk '!seen[$0]++'` removes duplicate lines while keeping the original order, which `sort -u` can't do.
concepts.code:
printf 'GET /a 200\nGET /b 404\nPOST /a 200\nGET /a 500\n' > req.log

# requests per path
awk '{ n[$2]++ } END { for (p in n) print p, n[p] }' req.log | sort
# /a 3
# /b 1

# count per status, most frequent first
awk '{ c[$3]++ } END { for (s in c) print s, c[s] }' req.log | sort -k2,2nr
# 200 2   (then 404 1 and 500 1)

# de-duplicate while keeping first-seen order
printf 'b\na\nb\nc\na\n' | awk '!seen[$0]++'     # b / a / c
takeaways: arr[key]++ and arr[key] += x build counts and sums per key
for (k in arr) has no guaranteed order: pipe to sort
!seen[$0]++ removes duplicates and keeps order
pitfalls: Testing arr[k] == "" to check membership, which silently creates the key; use (k in arr).

quiz.q: What does awk '!seen[$1]++' print?
options: Lines whose first field appears more than once
The first line for each distinct first field
The count of each first field
Only the last line for each first field
quiz.explain: !seen[$1]++ is true only when seen[$1] was still 0, which is the first time that value appears.

concepts.name: sort, uniq, cut and tr
concepts.summary: The helper filters that finish most pipelines: sort lines, count duplicates with uniq -c, cut out columns and translate characters.
concepts.why: grep, sed and awk find and reshape data; these helpers rank, count and tidy it into an answer.
concepts.body:
A few small standard commands (on Linux, from the GNU coreutils package) appear in almost every text pipeline:

- `sort` orders lines. `-n` sorts as numbers, `-r` reverses, `-h` understands sizes like `2K` and `1G`, `-u` keeps one of each, `-t ','` sets the separator, `-k2,2` sorts by field 2 only. Always write the end of the key (`-k2,2`): `-k2` means from field 2 to the end of the line.
- `uniq` merges duplicate lines that are **next to each other**, so it nearly always comes after `sort`. `uniq -c` puts counts in front, `-d` shows only duplicated lines.
- `cut` pulls out columns split on a **delimiter**, a separator character (`cut -d, -f1,3`), or by character position (`cut -c1-8`). Unlike awk it treats every delimiter as a separator, so two spaces in a row mean an empty field between them.
- `tr` translates or deletes characters: `tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'` upper-cases, `tr -d '\r'` removes the extra `\r` character Windows puts at line ends, `tr -s ' '` squeezes repeated spaces into one.
- `head -n`, `tail -n` and `wc -l` take the top, the bottom and the count.

The "top N" pattern combines them:

```bash
... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

It counts each distinct line, then ranks by count.

`sort` follows your **locale**: the language and region settings that decide, among other things, alphabetical order. With `LC_ALL=C sort` you get plain byte order (by each character's code number), which is faster and identical on every machine. That matters when another tool, like `join` or `comm`, expects sorted input.
concepts.code:
printf '10.0.0.1 GET\n10.0.0.2 GET\n10.0.0.1 POST\n10.0.0.1 GET\n' > hits.txt

# top client addresses
cut -d' ' -f1 hits.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#       3 10.0.0.1
#       1 10.0.0.2

printf 'b,2\na,10\nc,1\n' | sort -t, -k2,2n     # c,1 / b,2 / a,10
printf 'b,2\na,10\nc,1\n' | sort -t, -k2,2      # c,1 / a,10 / b,2  (text order!)

echo 'Hello,   World' | tr -s ' ' | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'   # HELLO, WORLD
printf 'line\r\n' | tr -d '\r' | od -c | head -1   # no \r left
takeaways: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head ranks the most common lines
uniq only merges lines that are next to each other, so sort first
Use -k2,2 with -n to sort numbers in one field
pitfalls: Sorting numbers without -n, so 10 comes before 2.

quiz.q: Why is sort usually placed before uniq?
options: uniq only removes duplicates that are next to each other
uniq needs alphabetical order to count
quiz.explain: uniq compares each line with the previous one, so equal lines must be adjacent.

concepts.name: sed: hold space and multi-line editing
concepts.summary: Work across lines in sed with N, D and P, the hold space (h, H, g, G, x) and labels with branching.
concepts.why: Joining continuation lines or editing a line based on its neighbour needs sed's multi-line commands.
concepts.body:
Normally sed sees one line at a time. A few commands widen the view:

- `N` appends the next input line to the pattern space, with a `\n` (line break) between them.
- `P` prints up to the first line break; `D` deletes up to the first line break and starts the next round of the script without reading a new line. `N;P;D` gives a sliding two-line window.
- The **hold space** is a second storage area that keeps its contents from one line to the next. `h` copies the pattern space into it, `H` appends to it, `g` copies it back, `G` appends it to the pattern space, `x` swaps the two.
- `:label` marks a spot in the script, `b label` jumps to it, and `t label` jumps only if a substitution succeeded since the last input line was read (or since the last `t`).

Common uses:

- `sed ':a; /\\$/ { N; s/\\\n//; ba }'` joins lines ending in a backslash with the next.
- `sed -n '1!G; h; $p'` reverses a file (what `tac` does).
- GNU sed's `-z` splits input on **NUL** characters (character code 0) instead of line breaks, so a normal text file becomes one big "line" that you can edit with patterns containing `\n`.

This is where sed programs become hard to read. If the logic needs more than a couple of these commands, an awk script, which has real variables and `if`, is usually clearer and easier to maintain.
concepts.code:
# join lines ending in a backslash with the next line
printf 'cmd --a \
  --b
next
' | sed -e ':a' -e '/\$/{N; s/\
 *//; ba' -e '}'
# cmd --a --b
# next

# reverse a file: prepend each line to the hold space, print at the end
printf '1
2
3
' | sed -n '1!G; h; $p'          # 3 / 2 / 1

# print each line that comes right before a line containing ERROR
printf 'a
b
ERROR
c
' | sed -n '$!N; /
ERROR/P; D'     # b

# -z: replace the newline between two lines
printf 'key=
value
' | sed -z 's/=
/=/'           # key=value
takeaways: N appends the next line; P and D work on the first line in the pattern space
h/H/g/G/x move text between the pattern space and the hold space
Switch to awk once a sed program needs more than a few of these
pitfalls: Forgetting that N on the last line prints and exits in GNU sed but behaves differently elsewhere; guard with $!N.

quiz.q: What does the D command do when the pattern space contains a line break?
options: Moves the pattern space to the hold space
Deletes the whole pattern space and reads the next line
Deletes up to the first line break and restarts the script with the rest
quiz.explain: D removes the first line only and restarts the script on what remains, without reading new input.

concepts.name: awk programs: printf, functions, two files
concepts.summary: Write real awk programs with printf, text functions, your own functions, -v variables, script files and two-file lookups via NR==FNR.
concepts.why: Beyond one-liners awk is a small, fast language for reports and data reshaping that runs everywhere.
concepts.body:
Longer programs go in a file and run with `awk -f report.awk data`. Pass shell values in with `-v name=value` instead of pasting them into the quoted program.

Useful built-ins:

- `printf` with `%s %d %.2f %-10s` for aligned columns; `sprintf` returns the text instead of printing it.
- Text functions: `length(s)`, `substr(s, start, len)` (positions start at 1), `index(s, t)`, `split(s, arr, sep)` which returns the number of pieces, `tolower`, `toupper`.
- `sub(re, repl [, target])` and `gsub(...)` replace in place and return the number of replacements; `&` in `repl` is the match. `match(s, re)` sets `RSTART` and `RLENGTH`.

You can write your own **functions**: named, reusable pieces of code, `function name(a, b,    tmp) { ... }`. Here `a` and `b` are **parameters**, the function's named inputs.

awk has no other way to declare **local variables**, ones that exist only inside the function, so by convention extra parameters listed after some spaces (`tmp` above) serve as locals. An array passed to a function is shared with the caller, so changes stick; a single value is copied.

With several input files, `FNR` is the line number within the current file while `NR` keeps counting. So `NR == FNR` is true only while reading the first file. This is the standard way to do lookups: load the first file into an array, then use it on the second.

gawk adds extras (`strftime`, `gensub`, `--csv`, sorted loops over arrays), but code using them won't run on **mawk** (the default awk on Debian and Ubuntu) or BSD awk.
concepts.code:
printf 'u1 Ana\nu2 Bo\n' > users.txt
printf 'u2 15.5\nu1 7\nu2 4.5\n' > orders.txt

# join: load users (first file), then total orders per user name
awk 'NR == FNR { name[$1] = $2; next }
     { total[name[$1]] += $2 }
     END { for (u in total) printf "%-5s %6.2f\n", u, total[u] }' users.txt orders.txt | sort
# Ana     7.00
# Bo     20.00

awk -v limit=10 '$2 > limit { print $1 }' orders.txt     # u2

awk 'function shout(s) { return toupper(s) "!" }
     { n = split($0, parts, "-"); print n, shout(parts[1]) }' <<< 'ab-cd-ef'
# 3 AB!
takeaways: Pass shell values with -v, longer programs with -f file.awk
NR == FNR { ...; next } loads the first file for a lookup
Extra function parameters are the way to declare local variables
pitfalls: Pasting a shell variable into the awk program text; quotes in the value break it. Use -v.

quiz.q: With awk '...' a.txt b.txt, when is NR == FNR true?
options: On every line of both files
quiz.explain: FNR resets for each file while NR doesn't, so they are equal only during the first file.

concepts.name: Safe filenames, xargs and locale
concepts.summary: Handle any filename with NUL separators (find -print0, grep -Z, xargs -0), and control behaviour and speed with LC_ALL.
concepts.why: Pipelines that work on test data often break on file names with spaces, or on a machine with different language settings.
concepts.code:
mkdir -p demo && cd demo
touch 'plain.log' 'with space.log' 'other.txt'
echo 'ERROR x' > 'with space.log'

# breaks: the name is split into "with" and "space.log"
find . -name '*.log' | xargs grep -l ERROR 2>/dev/null

# safe: NUL-separated names end to end
find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l ERROR      # ./with space.log
grep -rlZ ERROR . | xargs -0 -I{} echo "found: {}"         # found: ./with space.log
find . -name '*.log' -exec wc -l {} +                      # also safe

# byte-order sorting, identical everywhere
printf 'b\nB\na\n' | LC_ALL=C sort                       # B / a / b
takeaways: Only NUL can't appear in a file name: use -print0, -Z and xargs -0
find -exec cmd {} + is a safe alternative to xargs
LC_ALL=C treats text as plain bytes: same results everywhere and often faster
pitfalls: Piping find output into a while read loop or xargs without -0 and breaking on names with spaces.

quiz.q: Why is find . -print0 | xargs -0 rm safer than find . | xargs rm?
options: Names are separated by NUL, which can't occur inside a filename
quiz.explain: Newlines and spaces can appear in names, NUL cannot, so NUL separation is unambiguous.

concepts.name: grep -P, ripgrep and smarter searching
concepts.summary: Use Perl-style patterns with grep -P (lookarounds, \d, \K) and know when ripgrep or git grep is the better search tool.
concepts.why: Some extractions need lookarounds, and in large code projects a tool that skips ignored files is dramatically faster.
concepts.body:
GNU grep's `-P` switches to **PCRE** (Perl-compatible regular expressions, the pattern style of the Perl language). That adds:

- shorthand character classes `\d` (digit), `\w` (word character), `\s` (space), and `\b` for a word boundary;
- lazy repetition like `.*?`, which matches as little as possible instead of as much as possible;
- **lookarounds**, which check what comes before or after without including it: `(?<=user=)\w+` matches the name after `user=` but not `user=` itself;
- `\K`, which drops everything matched so far from the reported match: `grep -oP 'id=\K\d+'` prints just the number.

`-P` is a GNU feature and may be missing in minimal builds; BSD and macOS grep don't support it. In scripts that must run everywhere, prefer `-E` plus sed or awk for extraction.

For searching code, two other tools are often better than `grep -r`:

- `git grep` searches only the files Git tracks in a repository (a project folder under Git's version control), very quickly, and can search older versions: `git grep TODO v1.0`.
- **ripgrep** (`rg`) searches folders by default and skips what you usually don't want: files listed in `.gitignore`, hidden files (names starting with a dot) and non-text files.
- ripgrep also searches with all processor cores at once, and its matching time grows only in step with the input, never explodes. Its options mirror grep's (`-i`, `-w`, `-l`, `-C`), and `-t py` limits it to one file type.

Keep plain `grep` for pipelines and for scripts that must run everywhere; use `rg` or `git grep` interactively in large repositories.
concepts.code:
printf 'user=ana id=17\nuser=bo id=204\n' > log.txt

grep -oP 'id=\K\d+' log.txt                 # 17 / 204
grep -oP '(?<=user=)\w+' log.txt            # ana / bo
grep -oP 'user=.*?(?= )' log.txt            # user=ana / user=bo  (lazy + look ahead)

# works everywhere, without -P
grep -oE 'id=[0-9]+' log.txt | cut -d= -f2   # 17 / 204

# in a Git repository:
#   git grep -n 'TODO'            files Git tracks only
#   rg -t py 'def main'           ripgrep: skips ignored files, uses all cores
takeaways: grep -P adds \d, lazy repetition, lookarounds and \K
-P is GNU-only: use -E with cut or sed in scripts that must run everywhere
git grep and ripgrep are faster for searching code and skip ignored files
pitfalls: Shipping a script that uses grep -P to macOS users, where it fails with an invalid option error.

quiz.q: What does grep -oP 'v=\K\d+' print for the line 'v=42;'?
quiz.explain: \K discards the text matched before it, so only the digits are reported.

concepts.name: awk semantics: strings, numbers and $0
concepts.summary: Understand awk's dual text/number values, how assigning a field rebuilds $0 with OFS, and how RS, FS and getline really behave.
concepts.why: These rules explain the surprising outputs that bite people once awk programs get serious.
concepts.body:
Every awk value is a string, a number, or a **strnum**: input that looks numeric (fields, `getline` results, `-v` values) compares as a number with other numbers. Constants like `"10"` are always strings, so `$1 == "10"` is a string comparison and `"10" < "9"` is true. Force a type with `x + 0` (number) or `x ""` (string). Numbers turn into strings using `CONVFMT` (default `%.6g`), which is why large or long decimal values may print rounded.

Fields and `$0` are linked:

- Assigning any field, even `$1 = $1`, **rebuilds** `$0` by joining the fields with `OFS`. That's the standard way to change separators: `awk -v OFS=, '{ $1 = $1; print }'`.
- Assigning `$0` splits it into fields again; assigning `NF` cuts the record short or extends it.
- Setting `$(NF+2)` creates an empty field in between.

Records are separated by `RS` (a line break by default). `RS = ""` turns on **paragraph mode**: records are separated by blank lines, and a line break always also separates fields. gawk allows a regular expression as `RS` and puts the matched text in `RT`.

`getline` has several forms that change different things (`getline` updates `$0`, `NF` and `NR`; `getline var < file` updates only `var`), and returns -1 on error. So `while ((getline line < f) > 0)` is the only safe loop.
concepts.code:
echo '10 9' | awk '{ print ($1 > $2) }'            # 1  numeric: both are strnum
awk 'BEGIN { print ("10" > "9") }'                 # 0  string comparison
awk 'BEGIN { x = "3.0"; print (x == 3), (x + 0 == 3) }'   # 0 1

echo 'a b c' | awk -v OFS=, '{ print }'            # a b c   ($0 untouched)
echo 'a b c' | awk -v OFS=, '{ $1 = $1; print }'   # a,b,c   (rebuilt)
echo 'a b c' | awk '{ NF = 2; print }'             # a b

# paragraph mode: one record per blank-line separated block
printf 'ana\n31\n\nbo\n25\n' | awk 'BEGIN { RS = "" } { print NR, $1, $2 }'
# 1 ana 31
# 2 bo 25
takeaways: Field input is a strnum; quoted constants always compare as strings
Assigning a field rebuilds $0 with OFS: $1 = $1 changes separators
RS = "" is paragraph mode; loop on (getline line < f) > 0
pitfalls: Writing while (getline line < file) without > 0: a missing file returns -1 and the loop never ends.

quiz.q: Why does echo 'a b' | awk -v OFS=- '{ print }' print 'a b' and not 'a-b'?
options: OFS must be set in BEGIN
$0 is only rebuilt with OFS after a field is assigned
quiz.explain: print with no arguments prints $0 unchanged; assigning a field such as $1 = $1 rebuilds it using OFS.

concepts.name: How grep is fast, and when it isn't
concepts.summary: Why grep beats a naive loop: skipping ahead on fixed text, DFA matching and big block reads, and what slows it down (backreferences, -P, locales).
concepts.why: Knowing what makes a search slow lets you search gigabytes in seconds instead of minutes.
concepts.body:
GNU grep is fast because it avoids doing full pattern work on most of the input:

- It pulls out a **required literal**, a piece of fixed text every match must contain (for `ERROR [0-9]+` that's `ERROR `), and looks for it with a Boyer-Moore-style search, which can jump ahead several bytes at a time. Only lines containing it are checked by the full matcher.
- The full matcher is a **DFA** (deterministic finite automaton): a lookup table built from the pattern, piece by piece as needed. Each input byte costs one table lookup and nothing is ever retried, so time grows only in step with the input size.
- It reads big blocks and doesn't split the input into lines first; it finds line boundaries only around matches.

Things that defeat this:

- **Backreferences** like `\(a*\)\1` can't be expressed as a DFA, so grep falls back to **backtracking**: trying one way to match, and on failure going back to try another. That can take exponentially long.
- `-P` uses PCRE2, which turns patterns into machine code on the fly: fast for typical patterns, but it backtracks, so badly written patterns can be very slow.
- Locales where characters take several bytes can force slower paths for some patterns; `LC_ALL=C` often speeds up large ASCII searches.
- `-i` in some locales, and patterns with no usable fixed text, also reduce the skipping.

For many fixed strings use `-F -f patterns.txt`: grep builds an Aho-Corasick-style matcher that searches for all of them in one pass. Avoid loops that run grep once per pattern over the same file.
concepts.code:
# 2 million lines of test data
seq 1 2000000 | sed 's/^/line /' > big.txt

time grep -c 'line 1999999' big.txt        # literal: skips most bytes
time LC_ALL=C grep -c 'line 1999999' big.txt

# many fixed strings in one pass instead of a loop of greps
printf 'line 17\nline 42\nline 99\n' > wanted.txt
grep -cxF -f wanted.txt big.txt            # 3

# backreference: no DFA possible, much slower on big inputs
time grep -cE '(1)\1' big.txt
takeaways: grep looks for a required piece of fixed text first, then confirms with a DFA
Backreferences and -P fall back to backtracking
Use -F -f file for many fixed strings in one pass
pitfalls: Looping over a list of terms and running grep once per term on the same large file.

quiz.q: Why are backreferences slow in grep?
options: They can't be matched by a DFA, so grep must backtrack
quiz.explain: A DFA keeps no memory of text captured earlier, so patterns with backreferences need a backtracking matcher.

concepts.name: POSIX, GNU and BSD differences
concepts.summary: Know which grep, sed and awk features are POSIX and which are GNU or BSD extras, so your scripts run on Linux, macOS and small containers.
concepts.why: A pipeline that works on your laptop can fail on macOS, in a small container or on a build server, because each ships different versions of these tools.
concepts.body:
The same command names hide different programs: GNU tools on most Linux systems, BSD tools on macOS and FreeBSD, **BusyBox** in Alpine Linux and many containers (small, isolated environments that apps are shipped and run in), and mawk as the default awk on Debian and Ubuntu.

Frequent gotchas:

- `sed -i`: GNU takes an optional suffix, BSD requires one. Use `-i.bak` or avoid `-i`.
- `sed`: `\n` in the replacement, the `I` flag, `\U`/`\L`, `-z`, the one-line `a text` and the `e` command are GNU-only. BSD sed needs the escaped-line-break form for `a\`.
- `grep`: `-P` is GNU-only. `\+ \? \|` in BRE are GNU extras; `-E` works everywhere.
- `\w`, `\s`, `\b` and `\<` are not POSIX; `[[:alnum:]_]` and `[[:space:]]` are.
- `awk`: `gensub`, `strftime`, `PROCINFO`, `--csv`, `asort`, `@include` (and `length(arr)` on older awks) are gawk extras; mawk and BSD awk lack most of them.
- `sort -h`, `xargs -0` and `find -print0` are widespread but not universal.

Strategies:

- Write to POSIX and test with the versions you target, for example by running your script in an `alpine` and a `debian` container.
- On macOS, install the GNU versions (`brew install gnu-sed gawk grep`, available as `gsed`, `gawk`, `ggrep`) if you need them, but don't assume your users have them.
- When a pipeline needs many extras, a small Python script is often the more portable choice.
concepts.code:
# portable                          # GNU-only equivalent
grep -E 'a+|b' f                    # grep 'a\+\|b' f
grep '[[:space:]]' f                # grep '\s' f
sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' f && rm f.bak   # sed -i 's/a/b/' f
sed 's/x/&\
/' f                                # sed 's/x/&\n/' f   (newline in replacement)
awk '{ print toupper($0) }' f       # gawk '{ print gensub(/a/, "b", "g") }' f

# which implementation am I using?
awk --version 2>/dev/null | head -1 || awk -W version 2>&1 | head -1
sed --version 2>/dev/null | head -1 || echo "not GNU sed (probably BSD)"
takeaways: macOS ships BSD sed and grep, Debian's default awk is mawk, Alpine uses BusyBox
POSIX character classes like [[:space:]] work everywhere; \s and \w don't
Test scripts on the versions of the tools you ship to
pitfalls: Testing a script only with GNU tools and shipping it to macOS users or Alpine containers.

quiz.q: Which of these works the same with GNU and BSD sed?
quiz.explain: Both accept an attached suffix for -i; the other forms are GNU-specific or interpreted differently.
